This program needs to. # `delete` answers the value that was there, or `nil`, and the entries # that remain keep their order - so a person who signs out and back in # goes to the end of the table, which is what a table of arrivals means. # Like `basics`, `inventory`, `config`, `grid` and `shapes`, this documents # no rule: it is here because the prelude grows only when a program asks # (SPEC.md 0.1.0 item 3), and forgetting is what the sixth program does. module samples/sessions struct Session property user : String property since : Int32 # the tick the session opened on def initialize(@user : String, @since : Int32) end end class Table @open : Hash(String, Session) @tick : Int32 def initialize @open = {} of String => Session @tick = 0 end def sign_in(user : String) : Nil @tick = @tick + 1 @open[user] = Session.new(user, @tick) end # The session that closed, or nil when nobody by that name was in. def sign_out(user : String) : Session? @open.delete(user) end def show : Nil @open.each { |user, session| puts " #{user} since tick #{session.since}" } puts " (#{@open.size} signed in)" end end table = Table.new table.sign_in("ada") table.sign_in("linus") table.sign_in("grace") puts "three arrivals:" table.show # => ada, linus, grace; 3 signed in if gone = table.sign_out("linus") puts "linus left, had been in since tick #{gone.since}" # => tick 2 end table.show # => ada, grace; 2 signed in puts "nobody named bob: #{table.sign_out("bob").nil?}" # => true # Back in, and at the end: an entry that was deleted is a new arrival. table.sign_in("linus") puts "linus is back:" table.show # => ada, grace, linus; 3 signed in # Deleting everything and refilling, so the table's growth and its index # are exercised past the first page of entries. 20.times { |i| table.sign_in("guest#{i}") } 20.times { |i| table.sign_out("guest#{i}") } table.show # => ada, grace, linus; 3 signed in
files.samples/iyi/shapes.iyi: # The first program with a trait of its own - shapes that answer their # area, held in one list, added up - and the arithmetic around it. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/shapes.iyi # # `hello` documents what a trait is. This is the program a person writes # once they know: two structs behind one trait, a list typed by the trait, # and the small arithmetic a program like it reaches for - a rounded float, # a sum over a block, a number parsed that may fail, a power, a shift, a loop # that ends on a `break`. Like `basics`, `inventory`, `config` and `grid`, # it documents no rule; the prelude grows only when a program in this # repository needs something (SPEC.md 0.1.0 item 3). module samples/shapes trait Shape # A requirement says so: `abstract`. A plain `def` here opens a body. abstract def area : Float64 abstract def name : String end struct Circle def initialize(@radius : Float64) end end impl Shape for Circle def area : Float64 3.14159 * @radius * @radius end def name : String "circle" end end struct Rect def initialize(@width : Float64, @height : Float64) end end impl Shape for Rect def area : Float64 @width * @height end def name : String "rect" end end # 1. One list, two kinds, each asked the same question. shapes = [Circle.new(1.0), Rect.new(2.0, 3.0)] of Shape shapes.each { |shape| puts "#{shape.name}: #{shape.area.round(2)}" } # => circle: 3.14 # => rect: 6.0 puts shapes.sum { |shape| shape.area }.round(1) # => 9.1 puts shapes.max_by { |shape| shape.area }.name # => rect # 2. Numbers that arrive as text, some of them wrong. inputs = ["12", "x", "7", "-3"] parsed = inputs.map { |text| text.to_i? } puts parsed # => [12, nil, 7, -3] puts parsed.compact.sum # => 16 puts parsed.compact.map(&.abs) # => [12, 7, 3] # 3. Powers, shifts, and a loop that decides when to stop. puts 2 ** 10, 2.0 ** -2 # => 1024, 0.25 puts 1_i64 << 40 # => 1099511627776 puts 1024 >> 3 # => 128 side = 0 loop do side += 1 break if side * side > 50 end puts side # => 8
files.samples/iyi/socket.iyi: # Sockets: TCP client and server in one program on loopback. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/socket.iyi # # Binds to an ephemeral port (port 0), connects, exchanges a message each way, # prints what arrived, and closes cleanly. module samples/socket import std/socket::{IyiSocket} # Server listens on an ephemeral port. The number the kernel picks is different # on every run, so it is used rather than printed: `bench/arena_exercise.sh` # runs every sample twice and asks for identical output, and a sample that # prints its port is a sample that can never answer that. server = IyiSocket.listen(0) port = server.local_port puts "server listening on an ephemeral port" # Client connects to server on loopback client = IyiSocket.connect("127.0.0.1", port).or_panic client.write("hello from client\n") # Server accepts and reads the message conn = server.accept.or_panic msg = conn.read(1024).or_panic puts "server received: #{msg}" # Server replies to client conn.write("hello from server\n") reply = client.read(1024).or_panic puts "client received: #{reply}" # Clean teardown client.close conn.close server.close puts "closed"
files.samples/iyi/std_iterator.iyi: # The `std/iterator` port, demonstrated — lazy sequences. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/std_iterator.iyi # # `std/iterator.iyi` holds the `Iterator` trait and its lazy adaptors. # Unlike `Enumerable`, which processes sequences eagerly and creates intermediate # arrays at each step, `Iterator` transforms elements on demand when pulled. module samples/std_iterator import std/traits::{Comparable, Num} import std/iterator::{Iterator, ArrayIterator, Stop} # An infinite sequence generator. Eagerly evaluating this would hang or OOM; # lazily evaluating it pulls only what the pipeline asks for. pub class NaturalNumbers getter pulls : Int32 def initialize @current = 1 @pulls = 0 end end impl Iterator for NaturalNumbers type Elem = Int32 def next : Int32 | Stop @pulls = @pulls + 1 val = @current @current = @current + 1 val end end # 1. Infinite sequence consumed finitely nats = NaturalNumbers.new first_five = nats.take(5).to_a puts "natural numbers first 5: #{first_five}" puts "pulls from generator: #{nats.pulls}" # 2. Composed lazy pipeline: square even naturals and take 4 # Eager evaluation would evaluate infinitely; lazy evaluation pulls only 8 items. nats2 = NaturalNumbers.new pipeline = nats2.select { |x| x % 2 == 0 } .map { |x| x * x } .take(4) .to_a puts "even squares first 4: #{pipeline}" puts "pulls for 4 matches: #{nats2.pulls}" # 3. Zipping and Chaining evens = Iterator.of([2, 4, 6]) odds = Iterator.of([1, 3, 5]) all_numbers = odds.chain(evens).to_a puts "chained odds and evens: #{all_numbers}" names = Iterator.of(["apple", "banana", "cherry"]) scores = Iterator.of([100, 95, 88]) pairs = names.zip(scores).to_a puts "zipped pairs: #{pairs}" # 4. Slicing and Windowing data = Iterator.of([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]) slices = data.each_slice(3).to_a puts "each_slice(3): #{slices}" window_source = Iterator.of([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]) windows = window_source.each_cons(3).to_a puts "each_cons(3): #{windows}" # 5. Stepping, Cycling, and Indexing stepped = Iterator.of([0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]).step(2).to_a puts "stepped by 2: #{stepped}" cycled = Iterator.of(["tick", "tock"]).cycle(2).to_a puts "cycled 2 times: #{cycled}" with_idx = Iterator.of(["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]).with_index(1).to_a puts "with_index(1): #{with_idx}" # 6. Terminals: fold, count, search nums = Iterator.of([10, 20, 30, 40]) sum = nums.reduce(0) { |acc, x| acc + x } puts "reduce sum: #{sum}" items = Iterator.of([1, 5, 12, 8, 3, 19]) greater_than_ten = items.find { |x| x > 10 } puts "first > 10: #{greater_than_ten}"
files.samples/iyi/std_text.iyi: # Standard text processing library demonstration. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/std_text.iyi import std/text # 1. Whitespace stripping and line cleaning raw_line = " \tGET /api/v1/users HTTP/1.1\r\n" cleaned = raw_line.strip.chomp puts "cleaned line: '#{cleaned}'" # 2. Splitting and partitioning parts = cleaned.split method = parts[0] path = parts[1] version = parts[2] puts "HTTP method: #{method}, path: #{path}, version: #{version}" key_val = "Authorization: Bearer token123".partition(": ") header_name = key_val[0] header_val = key_val[2] puts "Header '#{header_name}' = '#{header_val}'" # 3. Substitutions and transformations slug = "Hello World! This is iyi std/text.".downcase.tr(" /.", "---").delete("!") puts "slug: #{slug}" # 4. UTF-8 multi-byte handling greeting = "héllo world" puts "greeting size: #{greeting.size} characters, #{greeting.bytesize} bytes" puts "reversed greeting: #{greeting.reverse}" # 5. Base conversion hex_color = "ff" puts "hex '#{hex_color}' to decimal: #{hex_color.to_i(16)}"
files.samples/iyi/std_time.iyi: # Demonstrates `std/time`: wall clock, monotonic stopwatch, civil calendar, and RFC 3339. # # Run via: # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/std_time.iyi module samples/std_time import std/time::{Time, Span} # 1. Fixed reference date demonstration ref_time = Time.utc(2024, 2, 29, 12, 30, 45, 123) puts "Reference time (UTC): #{ref_time.to_s}" puts "RFC 3339: #{ref_time.to_rfc3339(3)}" puts "Unix timestamp: #{ref_time.to_unix} s (#{ref_time.to_unix_ms} ms)" # 2. Civil calendar components puts "Year: #{ref_time.year}" puts "Month: #{ref_time.month}" puts "Day: #{ref_time.day}" puts "Day of week: #{ref_time.day_of_week.to_s}" puts "Day of year: #{ref_time.day_of_year}" # 3. Time arithmetic with Span one_day = Span.days(1_i64) tomorrow = ref_time + one_day yesterday = ref_time - one_day puts "Tomorrow: #{tomorrow.to_rfc3339}" puts "Yesterday: #{yesterday.to_rfc3339}" # 4. Live clock queries (wall clock and monotonic stopwatch) now = Time.utc puts "Live wall clock valid: #{now.year >= 2024}" start = Time.monotonic # Burn a few cycles to measure elapsed duration acc = 0_i64 i = 0 while i < 100000 acc = acc + i.to_i64 i = i + 1 end elapsed = Time.monotonic - start puts "Monotonic duration >= 0: #{elapsed.total_seconds >= 0.0}" # 5. Parsing RFC 3339 strings event = Time.parse_rfc3339("2024-02-29T12:00:00Z") puts "Leap day event: #{event.to_s}" puts "Is leap year: #{Time.leap_year?(event.year)}"
files.samples/iyi/visited.iyi: # The first program that remembers what it has seen - a walk over a graph # with cycles in it, which ends only because it keeps a set of where it # has been. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/visited.iyi # # A `Hash` answers "what is this key's value"; a walk asks a smaller # question, "have I been here", and asks it of every neighbour of every # node. `Set` is that question with nothing attached to the answer: `add` # says whether the element was new, which is the one bit a walk needs, # and the set prints in the order things went in, so the path reads back # as a path. Like the six programs before it, this documents no rule: it # is here because the prelude grows only when a program asks (SPEC.md # 0.1.0 item 3), and the seventh program asks for a set. module samples/visited # Who links to whom. `docs` links back to `home`, which is the cycle a # walk without memory would never leave. links = { "home" => ["docs", "blog"], "docs" => ["install", "home"], "blog" => ["docs", "about"], "install" => [] of String, "about" => ["home"], "orphan" => ["home"], } of String => Array(String) # Everything reachable from `start`, breadth first, each page once. def reachable(links : Hash(String, Array(String)), start : String) : Set(String) seen = Set(String).new seen.add(start) queue = [start] while page = queue.shift? (links[page]? || [] of String).each do |next_page| queue << next_page if seen.add(next_page) end end seen end from_home = reachable(links, "home") puts from_home # => Set{"home", "docs", "blog", "install", "about"} puts from_home.size # => 5 puts from_home.includes?("orphan") # => false puts reachable(links, "install") # => Set{"install"} # The pages nobody reaches from home, which is the set difference. everything = Set(String).new links.each { |page, _| everything.add(page) } puts everything - from_home # => Set{"orphan"} # `add` answers whether the element was new: the second time is false. tags = Set(String).new puts tags.add("iyi") # => true puts tags.add("iyi") # => false puts tags.delete("iyi") # => true puts tags.empty? # => true # And the everyday shape of the same question: a list with repeats, # read into a set and back out, first occurrence wins. words = "the cat and the dog and the bird".split(' ') puts words.to_set.to_a # => ["the", "cat", "and", "dog", "bird"]
files.samples/iyi/webapp.iyi: # The Sinatra feel, kept — but written by the consumer rather than injected by # the library. This is the whole argument of SPEC.md II.3 in one file. module samples/webapp import kemal/dsl::* import kemal/router::{Router, Context} before_all do |env| nil end get "/" do |env| "home" end get "/users" do |env| "all users" end post "/users" do |env| "created" end # A route may return anything implementing `IntoBody`, which is strictly more # than Kemal allows: Kemal coerces non-String results to "" at runtime. get "/count" do |env| 42 end # A route returning a type with no impl is refused where it is written: # # get "/bad" do |env| # [1, 2, 3] # end # # => Array(Int32) does not implement Kemal::Router::IntoBody, # # required by `B` in `get` # # Kemal cannot say this. `HTTP::Server::Context -> _` accepts the block and # silently returns an empty body on every request. users = Router.new users.get "/" do |env| "users index" end # The sub-router is a block parameter rather than the block's `self`: R-2 asks # an exported `def` to describe its block, and a block whose `self` changes is # the one shape no annotation can describe yet. See `kemal/router.iyi`. users.namespace "/admin" do |admin| admin.get "/dashboard" do |env| "dashboard" end end mount "/v1", users app.routes.each { |route| puts "#{route[0]} #{route[1]}" } puts app.dispatch(Context.new("GET", "/count"))
files.samples/iyi/workers.iyi: # The first program with tasks in it - SPEC.md III.4, as a person writes it. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/workers.iyi # # Two shapes cover most of what a program wants from concurrency. A pool: # jobs go down one channel, workers answer up another, and the group's end # is the join. A pair: two things fetched at once, the group typed by what # they answer, so an error from either leaves as an ordinary member of the # union (III.4.3, III.4.9). Nothing here is a rule the other samples do not # state; it is the two programs a person writes first. module samples/workers # 1. A pool of three workers over six jobs. jobs = Channel(Int32).new(8) results = Channel(Int32).new(8) group do |g| 3.times do g.spawn do loop do case jobs.receive in Int32 then results.send(it * it) in ChannelClosed then break # no more jobs: this worker is done in Cancelled then break end end 0 end end g.spawn do (1..6).each { |n| jobs.send(n) } jobs.close 0 end total = 0 6.times do case results.receive in Int32 then total += it in ChannelClosed then break in Cancelled then break end end puts total # => 91, the squares of one to six end # The group's `end` waited for every worker: none outlives the scope that # started it (III.4.1). # 2. Two fetches at once, and the pair or the first error. struct Timeout def initialize(@what : String) end end impl Error for Timeout def message : String "#{@what} timed out" end end def read(name : String) : String | Timeout return Timeout.new(name) if name == "slow" "<#{name}>" end # `end!` makes the group a value: the tuple of what the two tasks answered, # or the first error member. `Panicked` is there because a task that panics # answers it (III.1.4), and the signature says so. def both(a : String, b : String) : Tuple(String, String) | Timeout | Panicked group do |g| x = g.spawn { read(a) } y = g.spawn { read(b) } end! end case both("one", "two") in Tuple(String, String) then puts it # => {"<one>", "<two>"} in Timeout then puts it.message in Panicked then puts "panicked" end case both("one", "slow") in Tuple(String, String) then puts it in Timeout then puts it.message # => slow timed out in Panicked then puts "panicked" end
files.samples/tour/arrays.iyi: # Arrays: ordered, growable, one element type. numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] puts numbers.size puts numbers[0] puts numbers.first puts numbers.last numbers << 9 # append puts numbers # The common questions. puts numbers.includes?(4) puts numbers.sum puts numbers.sorted puts numbers.select { |n| n > 2 } puts numbers.map { |n| n * 10 } puts numbers.reduce(0) { |acc, n| acc + n } # An empty array needs its element type written down. names = [] of String names << "Ayşe" names << "Mehmet" puts names.join(", ") # Walk with an index. names.each_with_index { |name, i| puts "#{i + 1}. #{name}" }
files.samples/tour/blocks.iyi: # Blocks and closures: code you hand to a function. # `yield` runs the block the caller passed. def repeat(times : Int32) times.times { |i| yield i } end repeat(3) { |i| puts "step #{i}" } # A block sees the variables around it. total = 0 [1, 2, 3].each { |n| total += n } puts total # `->` makes a function value you can store and call later. square = ->(x : Int32) { x * x } puts square.call(7) # It captures its surroundings too: this one counts every call. count = 0 tick = ->() { count += 1 } tick.call tick.call puts count # A block parameter with a type, handed on as a value. def apply(x : Int32, &f : Int32 -> Int32) : Int32 f.call(x) end puts apply(5) { |v| v + 100 }
files.samples/tour/bounds.iyi: # Bounds: a generic that asks its type parameter for a trait. trait Priced abstract def price : Int32 end struct Book def initialize(@price : Int32) end end struct Coffee def initialize(@price : Int32) end end impl Priced for Book def price : Int32 @price end end impl Priced for Coffee def price : Int32 @price end end # `T : Priced` says: any T, as long as it implements Priced. The bound is # checked where the call is made, so `total([1, 2])` would not compile. def total(items : Array(T)) : Int32 forall T : Priced items.sum { |item| item.price } end puts total([Book.new(120), Book.new(80)]) puts total([Coffee.new(45)]) def cheapest(items : Array(T)) : T forall T : Priced items.min_by { |item| item.price } end puts cheapest([Coffee.new(45), Coffee.new(30)]).price
files.samples/tour/case.iyi: # `case`: one value, many branches. def day_kind(day : String) : String case day when "Saturday", "Sunday" then "weekend" when "Friday" then "almost" else "weekday" end end puts day_kind("Sunday") puts day_kind("Friday") puts day_kind("Tuesday") # A `case` with no value tests each condition in turn. score = 87 case when score >= 90 then puts "A" when score >= 80 then puts "B" else puts "C" end # `case ... in` matches on type, and it must cover every possibility. # `it` is the value, already narrowed to the branch's type. value = score > 50 ? 1 : "one" case value in Int32 then puts "a number: #{it + 1}" in String then puts "a word: #{it.upcase}" end
files.samples/tour/channels.iyi: # Channels: tasks talk by sending values, not by sharing them. jobs = Channel(Int32).new(8) results = Channel(Int32).new(8) group do |g| # Two workers. Each takes jobs until the channel closes. 2.times do g.spawn do loop do case jobs.receive in Int32 then results.send(it * 10) in ChannelClosed then break in Cancelled then break end end 0 end end # One producer. Closing says there will be no more. g.spawn do (1..5).each { |n| jobs.send(n) } jobs.close 0 end # Collect five answers. total = 0 5.times do case results.receive in Int32 then total += it in ChannelClosed then break in Cancelled then break end end puts total end
files.samples/tour/classes.iyi: # A class is a reference: two names can point at one object. class Counter # `property` makes a field readable and writable from outside. property count : Int32 def initialize(@count : Int32) end def bump : Nil @count += 1 end end a = Counter.new(0) b = a # b is the same counter, not a copy b.bump b.bump puts a.count # 2: the change is visible through a # A struct behaves differently: `b = a` would copy, and `a` stays at 0. # Use a struct for small values, a class for things that have identity. struct Cell property value : Int32 def initialize(@value : Int32) end end x = Cell.new(0) y = x y.value = 5 puts x.value # 0
files.samples/tour/conditions.iyi: # Conditions: `if`, `elsif`, `else`, `unless`, and `if` as a value. temperature = 23 if temperature > 30 puts "hot" elsif temperature > 20 puts "warm" else puts "cold" end # `unless` is `if not`. unless temperature < 0 puts "above freezing" end # A one-line form goes after the statement. puts "nice day" if temperature == 23 # `if` is an expression, so it can be assigned. label = if temperature > 20 "warm" else "cool" end puts label # The short form: condition ? when true : when false. puts temperature.even? ? "even" : "odd" # `&&`, `||`, `!` combine conditions. puts temperature > 20 && temperature < 30 puts !(temperature > 20)
files.samples/tour/constants.iyi: # Constants: a capitalised name, assigned once. PI = 3.14159 GREETING = "Merhaba" LIMIT = 100 def circle_area(r : Float64) : Float64 PI * r * r end puts circle_area(2.0).round(2) puts "#{GREETING}, dünya" puts LIMIT > 99
files.samples/tour/conversions.iyi: # Conversions are explicit: nothing changes type on its own. n = 42 puts n.to_f puts n.to_s + "!" f = 9.99 puts f.to_i puts f.round(1) # From text. `to_i` expects a number; `to_i?` answers nil when there is none. puts "17".to_i + 1 puts "17".to_i? puts "seventeen".to_i? # A Char is a byte, and its code is a number. puts 'A'.ord puts 66.chr
files.samples/tour/defaults.iyi: # Default methods: a trait can carry bodies of its own. trait Greet abstract def name : String # Not abstract: every implementer gets this one for free, written in # terms of the requirement. def greeting : String "Merhaba, #{name}!" end def shout : String greeting.upcase end end struct Person def initialize(@name : String) end end impl Greet for Person def name : String @name end end struct Robot def initialize(@id : Int32) end end impl Greet for Robot def name : String "unit #{@id}" end # An implementer may replace a default. def greeting : String "BEEP #{name}" end end puts Person.new("Ada").greeting puts Person.new("Ada").shout puts Robot.new(7).greeting puts Robot.new(7).shout
files.samples/tour/defer.iyi: # `defer`: name the cleanup where you acquire, run it when the scope ends. def work : Int32 puts "open" defer puts "close" puts "working" 42 end puts work # Deferred lines run last-in, first-out. def nested : Nil defer puts "third" defer puts "second" puts "first" end nested # The scope is the block, so in a loop the cleanup runs every turn. 2.times do |i| defer puts "done with #{i}" puts "turn #{i}" end
files.samples/tour/dispatch.iyi: # A trait is a type: one list, many kinds, one question. trait Speak abstract def sound : String end struct Dog def initialize(@name : String) end def name : String @name end end struct Cat def initialize(@name : String) end def name : String @name end end impl Speak for Dog def sound : String "hav" end end impl Speak for Cat def sound : String "miyav" end end # `of Speak` types the array by the trait, so both fit. animals = [Dog.new("Karabaş"), Cat.new("Pamuk")] of Speak animals.each { |animal| puts animal.sound } # A function can ask for the trait rather than a particular type. def chorus(voices : Array(Speak)) : String voices.map { |v| v.sound }.join(" ") end puts chorus(animals)
files.samples/tour/errors.iyi: # Errors are values. A function that can fail says so in its type. struct NotFound def initialize(@key : String) end def key : String @key end end # `Error` is a trait the compiler knows. Implementing it makes a type an # error member wherever it appears in a union. impl Error for NotFound def message : String "no such key: #{key}" end end STORE = {"name" => "iyi", "year" => "2026"} def fetch(key : String) : String | NotFound STORE[key]? || NotFound.new(key) end # `!` propagates: a good value continues, an error returns from here. def year_plus_one : Int32 | NotFound text = fetch("year")! text.to_i + 1 end puts year_plus_one # Handle with `case`, or fall back with `.or`, or insist with `.or_panic`. case fetch("missing") in String then puts it in NotFound then puts it.message end puts fetch("missing").or("default") puts fetch("name").or_panic
files.samples/tour/exports.iyi: # `import x::{...}`: bring a module's exported names in, unqualified. # The whole surface with `::*`, or a chosen few in braces. Either way it is # this file that asks: a library cannot put names into a file that did not. import geometry/point::{Point, distance} home = Point.new(0, 0) work = Point.new(3, 4) puts distance(home, work) # `secret` was declared without `pub`, so it is not there to be found. # Uncomment the next line to see the compiler say so: # puts Geometry::Point.secret
files.samples/tour/functions.iyi: # Functions: `def`, typed parameters, a typed result. def add(a : Int32, b : Int32) : Int32 a + b end # The last expression is the result. There is no `return` needed. def describe(n : Int32) : String if n < 0 "negative" elsif n == 0 "zero" else "positive" end end # Parameters can have defaults, and callers can name them. def greet(name : String, greeting = "Hello") : String "#{greeting}, #{name}!" end puts add(2, 3) puts describe(-5) puts greet("Ayşe") puts greet("Ayşe", greeting: "Selam")
files.samples/tour/generic-functions.iyi: # Generic functions: `forall T` makes a function work for any type. def first(items : Array(T)) : T forall T items[0] end puts first([10, 20, 30]) puts first(["a", "b"]) def swap(pair : Tuple(A, B)) : Tuple(B, A) forall A, B {pair[1], pair[0]} end puts swap({1, "one"}) # The type is fixed per call: `first` of an Int32 array is an Int32, so # arithmetic on the result compiles. puts first([1, 2]) + 100
files.samples/tour/generic-types.iyi: # Generic types: a struct with a type parameter. struct Stack(T) def initialize @items = [] of T end def push(item : T) : Nil @items << item end def pop : T? @items.empty? ? nil : @items.pop end def size : Int32 @items.size end end numbers = Stack(Int32).new numbers.push(1) numbers.push(2) puts numbers.size puts numbers.pop puts numbers.pop puts numbers.pop words = Stack(String).new words.push("iyi") puts words.pop # A trait can be implemented for the generic type once, for every T. trait Describe abstract def describe : String end impl Describe for Stack(T) forall T def describe : String "a stack of #{size}" end end numbers.push(5) puts numbers.describe puts words.describe
files.samples/tour/geometry/point.iyi: # A module other files can import. Its path is its name. module geometry/point # `pub` makes a declaration part of the module's surface. An exported # declaration writes its types down, so a file that imports this one # never has to read the body. pub struct Point getter x : Int32 getter y : Int32 def initialize(@x : Int32, @y : Int32) end end pub def distance(a : Point, b : Point) : Int32 (a.x - b.x).abs + (a.y - b.y).abs end # No `pub`: this name is the module's own and cannot be reached from outside. def secret : String "only here" end
files.samples/tour/hashes.iyi: # Hashes: keys to values, in insertion order. ages = {"Ayşe" => 31, "Mehmet" => 27} puts ages["Ayşe"] puts ages.size ages["Zeynep"] = 40 puts ages.keys # `[]?` answers nil for a missing key instead of failing. puts ages["Ali"]? puts ages.has_key?("Ali") ages.each do |name, age| puts "#{name} is #{age}" end # An empty hash needs both types written down. counts = {} of String => Int32 ["a", "b", "a"].each do |letter| counts[letter] = (counts[letter]? || 0) + 1 end puts counts
files.samples/tour/hello.iyi: # Your first iyi program. puts "Hello Türkiye!"
files.samples/tour/loops.iyi: # Loops: `each` over a collection, `times`, `while`, and `loop`. [1, 2, 3].each do |n| puts n end 3.times { |i| puts "round #{i}" } n = 1 while n < 50 n = n * 2 end puts n # `loop` runs until `break`. `next` skips to the next turn. count = 0 loop do count += 1 next if count == 2 puts "count #{count}" break if count == 4 end
files.samples/tour/methods.iyi: # Methods: functions that belong to a type. struct Rectangle getter width : Float64 getter height : Float64 def initialize(@width : Float64, @height : Float64) end def area : Float64 width * height end def square? : Bool width == height end # A method can take arguments like any function. def scale(factor : Float64) : Rectangle Rectangle.new(width * factor, height * factor) end end r = Rectangle.new(3.0, 4.0) puts r.area puts r.square? puts r.scale(2.0).area # Methods on the built-in types work the same way. puts "iyi".upcase puts 3.7.round puts [1, 2, 3].sum
files.samples/tour/modules.iyi: # Modules: every file is one, and `import` brings another in. # `geometry/point` is the file geometry/point.iyi. The path is the name. import geometry/point # After `import`, the module's exports are reachable under its qualified # name: the path with each segment capitalised, joined by `::`. a = Geometry::Point::Point.new(1, 2) b = Geometry::Point::Point.new(4, 6) puts Geometry::Point.distance(a, b)
files.samples/tour/nil.iyi: # nil is a value, and the type says whether it can appear. # `String?` is `String | Nil`: it may hold a string, or nothing. def lookup(id : Int32) : String? id == 1 ? "Ada" : nil end found = lookup(1) missing = lookup(2) puts found puts missing # Before you use a maybe-nil value, check it. Inside the `if`, the # compiler knows it is a String. if found puts found.upcase end # Or give a default with `||`. puts missing || "nobody" # Calling a String method on a `String?` without checking does not # compile. That is the whole point: a nil can never surprise you at run time.
files.samples/tour/ranges.iyi: # Ranges: `..` includes the end, `...` stops before it. (1..5).each { |i| puts i } (1...5).each { |i| puts i } # A range is a collection: map, sum, select, to_a all work. puts (1..5).map { |i| i * i } puts (1..100).sum puts (1..10).select { |i| i % 3 == 0 } # Ranges also work in a `case`. age = 42 case age when 0..12 then puts "child" when 13..19 then puts "teen" else puts "adult" end
files.samples/tour/returns.iyi: # More than one result: a tuple, unpacked at the call. def divide(a : Int32, b : Int32) : Tuple(Int32, Int32) {a // b, a % b} end quotient, remainder = divide(17, 5) puts quotient puts remainder # A tuple is a value like any other. pair = divide(9, 4) puts pair[0] puts pair[1] # `return` leaves early, and can carry a value. def first_even(numbers : Array(Int32)) : Int32? numbers.each do |n| return n if n % 2 == 0 end nil end puts first_even([1, 3, 6, 7]) puts first_even([1, 3])
files.samples/tour/strings.iyi: # Strings, and `to_s`: how a type says what it looks like. s = "Hello, iyi" puts s.size puts s.upcase puts s.downcase puts s.includes?("iyi") puts s + "!" puts s.split(' ') # Interpolation calls `to_s` on whatever is inside `#{}`. puts "#{1 + 1} and #{true} and #{[1, 2]}" # Give your own type a `to_s`, and it prints the way you say. struct Money def initialize(@lira : Int32, @kurus : Int32) end def to_s : String "#{@lira},#{@kurus.to_s.rjust(2, '0')} TL" end end price = Money.new(12, 5) puts price.to_s puts "total: #{price}" # Padding lines up columns. puts "item".ljust(8) + "12" puts "total".ljust(8) + "99"
files.samples/tour/structs.iyi: # A struct: named fields, a constructor, methods. struct Point getter x : Int32 getter y : Int32 # `@x` is the field. Writing it in the parameter list assigns it. def initialize(@x : Int32, @y : Int32) end def +(other : Point) : Point Point.new(x + other.x, y + other.y) end def to_s : String "(#{x}, #{y})" end end a = Point.new(1, 2) b = Point.new(3, 4) puts a.x puts (a + b).to_s # A struct is a value: assigning it copies it. c = a puts c.to_s
files.samples/tour/tasks.iyi: # Tasks: run work at the same time, inside a group that waits for it all. def slow_square(n : Int32) : Int32 sleep 10 # milliseconds n * n end # `group` opens a scope. Every `spawn` inside it is a task, and the # group's `end` waits for every one of them: no task outlives its group. results = [] of Int32 group do |g| (1..4).each do |n| g.spawn do results << slow_square(n) 0 end end end puts results.sorted # `end!` turns the group into a value: the tuple of what its tasks answered. def both : Tuple(String, String) | Panicked group do |g| a = g.spawn { "first" } b = g.spawn { "second" } end! end case both in Tuple(String, String) then puts it in Panicked then puts "a task panicked" end
files.samples/tour/traits.iyi: # A trait: a set of methods a type promises to have. trait Shape # `abstract def` is a requirement. Every implementer must define it. abstract def area : Float64 end struct Circle def initialize(@radius : Float64) end end struct Square def initialize(@side : Float64) end end # `impl Trait for Type` is the one way to give a type a trait. The impl # lives next to the trait or next to the type, never anywhere else. impl Shape for Circle def area : Float64 3.14159 * @radius * @radius end end impl Shape for Square def area : Float64 @side * @side end end puts Circle.new(1.0).area.round(2) puts Square.new(2.0).area # Leave a requirement out and the compiler refuses the impl, naming the # missing method. Try removing `area` from one of the impls above.
files.samples/tour/tuples.iyi: # Tuples: a fixed group of values, each with its own type. pair = {1, "one"} puts pair[0] puts pair[1] # Unpack into variables. number, word = pair puts "#{number} is #{word}" # A named tuple gives each slot a name. person = {name: "Ayşe", age: 31} puts person[:name] puts person[:age] # A function that answers several things at once. def min_max(items : Array(Int32)) : Tuple(Int32, Int32) low = items.first high = items.first items.each do |n| low = n if n < low high = n if n > high end {low, high} end low, high = min_max([7, 2, 9, 4]) puts "#{low}..#{high}"
files.samples/tour/types.iyi: # The basic types, and what each literal is. i = 42 # Int32 big = 4_000_000_000_i64 # Int64, with a suffix f = 3.14 # Float64 b = true # Bool c = 'a' # Char s = "text" # String puts typeof(i) puts typeof(big) puts typeof(f) puts typeof(b) puts typeof(c) puts typeof(s) # Integer arithmetic stays integer with `//`; `/` gives a Float64. puts 7 // 2 puts 7 / 2 puts 7 % 2 puts 2 ** 10
files.samples/tour/unions.iyi: # Union types: a value that is one of several types. # `Int32 | String` holds either. Nothing is wrapped or boxed. def parse(text : String) : Int32 | String n = text.to_i? n ? n : "not a number: #{text}" end # `case ... in` must name every member, so a new member in the union # turns every incomplete `case` into a compile error. ["12", "x", "7"].each do |text| case parse(text) in Int32 then puts "number #{it * 2}" in String then puts "problem, #{it}" end end # `is_a?` asks, and narrows inside the `if`. value = parse("5") if value.is_a?(Int32) puts value + 1 end # `String?` from the nil lesson is the same idea: `String | Nil`.
files.samples/tour/variables.iyi: # Variables: assign a value and the type follows. name = "iyi" year = 2026 ratio = 0.75 ready = true puts name puts year puts ratio puts ready # A variable keeps its type. You can reassign, but not to a different kind. year = year + 1 puts year # Write the type when you want to be explicit. count : Int32 = 10 puts count
files.records/break/dep/global_derive.iyi: # A module the break program imports, exporting one derive macro. It compiles: # a macro body is expanded where the `derive` is written, not where the macro # is defined, so the refusal this module earns lands in its consumer's build. # # `counted` asks a question about the whole program. `all_subclasses` answers # with every type compiled beside it, which is exactly what R-5 keeps a macro # away from: a derive that read it would generate different code depending on # what else happened to be in the build, and then a `.iyimod` could not carry # what it generated (SPEC.md R-5, II.4). module dep/global_derive pub macro counted(declaration) def counted : Int32 {% count = 0 %} {% for field in declaration[:fields] %} {% count = field[:type].all_subclasses.size %} {% end %} {{ count }} end end
files.records/break/dep/greeter.iyi: # A module the break programs import. Its surface is deliberately narrow: one # exported function, one exported trait, and one function left unexported so a # consumer has something it is not allowed to reach. module dep/greeter pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub def polite(name : String) : String "#{greeting}, #{name}." end # No `pub`, so this is the module's own business. It is not in the module's # declarations, which is what makes reaching for it from another module an # error rather than a style question (SPEC.md R-1, IV.2). def greeting : String "Hello" end
files.records/break/dep/loop_a.iyi: # Half of a deliberate import cycle. See `../r1_import_cycle.iyi`. module dep/loop_a import dep/loop_b pub def a : String "a" end
files.records/break/dep/loop_b.iyi: # The other half of the cycle. `dep/loop_a` imports this module and this # module imports `dep/loop_a`, which is the edge that closes it. module dep/loop_b import dep/loop_a pub def b : String "b" end
files.records/break/dep/user.iyi: # A second module the break programs import, so that a trait and a type can # live in two different places and an impl can be written in a third. module dep/user pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end
files.records/break/errors_non_exhaustive.iyi: # Breaks the error rule in SPEC.md III.1: an error is an ordinary member of a # union, so handling one needs no new machinery, only the totality check a # `case` already performs. `read` can return an `IOError` and this `case` has # no branch for it, which is the same mistake as ignoring a returned error and # is caught by the same check. module diagnostics/errors_non_exhaustive pub struct IOError getter path : String def initialize(@path : String) end end # `Error` is the compiler's trait, which is what lets a union member be an # error member without any name in scope deciding it. impl Error for IOError def message : String "no such file: #{path}" end end pub def read(path : String) : String | IOError return IOError.new(path) if path == "missing" "12" end case read("missing") in String then puts it end
files.records/break/r1_import_cycle.iyi: # Breaks R-1: a module is the unit of compilation and `import` forms a DAG, so # the graph has to be acyclic for anything else to hold. A cycle has no # initialisation order, since a module initialises after every module it # imports and here each would have to follow the other, and the acyclicity is # also what makes at most one module able to define any given impl. `dep/loop_a` # and `dep/loop_b` import each other. module diagnostics/r1_import_cycle import dep/loop_a::* puts a
files.records/break/r2_missing_return_type.iyi: # Breaks R-2: everything a module exports carries full parameter and return # types, because the signature is the whole of what a consumer reads. Drop the # return type and there is nothing to write into the artifact, so the omission # is refused where it is written rather than inferred from the body. module diagnostics/r2_missing_return_type pub def total(numbers : Array(Int32)) numbers.sum end puts total([1, 2, 3])
files.records/break/r2_not_exported.iyi: # Breaks R-2: only what a module marks `pub` is reachable from outside it, and # `greeting` in `dep/greeter` carries no `pub`. Qualifying the call does not get # around that. It has to be genuinely unreachable rather than merely left out # of an import's names, because a `.iyimod` carries a module's exports and nothing # else, so if another module could call an unmarked name that artifact would # not be enough to compile against. module diagnostics/r2_not_exported import dep/greeter puts Dep::Greeter.greeting
files.records/break/r2_wrong_return_type.iyi: # Breaks R-2 the other way: the type is written, and the body does not honour # it. An exported signature is a promise to every consumer that reads the # artifact instead of the body, so the body is the thing that has to give. module diagnostics/r2_wrong_return_type pub def total(numbers : Array(Int32)) : Int32 numbers.join(",") end puts total([1, 2, 3])
files.records/break/r2b_name_not_imported.iyi: # Breaks R-2b: a bare `import` brings a module into scope under its qualified # name and nothing more. Unqualified names arrive only through the list or the # glob on an import line, `::{...}` or `::*`, which the consumer writes, so # importing a module never quietly changes what a name in this file means. # `polite` is exported and still not in scope here. module diagnostics/r2b_name_not_imported import dep/greeter puts polite("iyi")
files.records/break/r2c_outside_bound.iyi: # Breaks R-2c: a def whose parameters and return are all written is typed at # its definition, caller or no caller, and a trait-restricted parameter is # typed against exactly its bound. Two halves of the rule fail here at once. # # Nothing in this file calls `loudest`, so under the lazy typing iyi inherited # from Crystal its body would never be visited and the build would report # itself clean. And `User`, the only implementer of `Greet` in the program, has # a `shout` of its own: duck-typed generics would have found it and compiled. # `Greet` declares `greet` and nothing else, so the body reaches outside the # bound it wrote down, and the message names the witness type the compiler # synthesized to type it (SPEC.md R-2c; # src/compiler/iyi/semantic/definition_typing.cr). module diagnostics/r2c_outside_bound pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end # Present on the concrete type, and irrelevant to the def below: the bound is # what that body is typed against, not whatever happens to implement it. def shout : String "HELLO" end end impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}." end end pub def loudest(g : Greet) : String g.shout end
files.records/break/r3_orphan_impl.iyi: # Breaks R-3: `impl Trait for Type` may live in the module that defines the # trait or the module that defines the type, and nowhere else. `Greet` belongs # to `dep/greeter` and `User` belongs to `dep/user`, so this module owns # neither and is the one place the impl cannot be written. That restriction is # what makes a type's method set knowable from its declarations alone. module diagnostics/r3_orphan_impl import dep/greeter::* import dep/user::* impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}." end end puts User.new("iyi").greet
files.records/break/r3_unmet_trait_bound.iyi: # Breaks R-3 from the calling side: a type's method set is closed, so a bound # on a type parameter is a question with a definite answer at the call. `Int32` # has no `impl Greet` and cannot acquire one later, so the call is refused as a # missing trait rather than as a failed overload match. module diagnostics/r3_unmet_trait_bound pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}." end end pub def announce(item : T) : String forall T : Greet "-> #{item.greet}" end puts announce(User.new("iyi")) puts announce(42)
files.records/break/r4_dictionary.iyi: # Breaks R-4 by asking for the one clause of it that has nothing behind it. # # R-4's third sentence says `@[Monomorphize]` forces specialisation across a # module boundary. SPEC.md III.9 records what that is worth today: nothing in # the compiler mentions the annotation, a dictionary or a GC shape. So this is # not a feature that misbehaves, it is a name the compiler has never heard, # and the rejection below is a compiler declining to accept a promise it # cannot keep rather than compiling the program as though the rule were built. # # What runs instead of the dictionary is the rule's second sentence applied # everywhere: a generic's body travels in the artifact and every consumer # compiles it again for the types it uses. `bench/generic_boundary.py` is the # measurement of what that costs a consumer's front end. module diagnostics/r4_dictionary @[Monomorphize] pub def twice(x : T) : Array(T) forall T [x, x] end puts twice(1).size
files.records/break/r5_global_question.iyi: # Breaks R-5: a macro sees the declaration it is attached to, and nothing # global. Everything here is legal. `Point` is this module's own type, the # derive is written inside its body where a derive belongs, and `counted` # is a name this file imports from another module, which is the only way a # derive macro can arrive. What is refused is the one question the macro asks: # `all_subclasses` answers with the whole program rather than with this # declaration, so the answer would depend on what else was compiled and the # methods it generated could not travel in this module's artifact. # # The refusal lands at expansion, in the consumer's build, which is where the # macro runs. `dep/global_derive.iyi` is the macro (SPEC.md R-5, II.4). module diagnostics/r5_global_question import dep/global_derive::* pub struct Point @x : Int32 def initialize(@x : Int32) end derive counted end puts Point.new(1).counted
files.records/agent/app/greeter.iyi: # The dependency. Its exported surface is the whole of what a consumer, or an # agent editing one, is allowed to know: two functions with their types # written down, and a trait. `greeting` has no `pub`, so it is this module's # own business and appears in no consumer's grounding (SPEC.md R-1, IV.2). module app/greeter pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end # The exported surface carries its doc comment, so the grounding pack an agent # reads says what the function is for and not only what it takes. pub def polite(name : String) : String "#{greeting}, #{name}." end pub def shout(name : String) : String "#{greeting.upcase}, #{name.upcase}!" end def greeting : String "Hello" end
files.records/agent/app.iyi: # The file being edited, in the state an agent meets it: one call misspelled. # The compiler knows the name it meant, so `iyi check -f json` carries a # `suggested_edit` with the exact replacement span and `iyi fix` applies it. module app import app/greeter::* pub def main : Int32 puts polit("Türkiye") 0 end
files.records/agent/app_test.iyi: # A test is a plain program that exits non-zero when it fails; the prelude's # `assert` is that in one word. No framework, so nothing here has to be # learned before it can be read. module app/app_test import app/greeter::* assert polite("iyi") == "Hello, iyi.", "polite greets" assert shout("iyi") == "HELLO, IYI!", "shout shouts"
files.records/agent/other.iyi: # Imported by nothing. It is here so `iyi test --affected` has a change it can # prove no test reaches, which is the half of test selection that is easy to # claim and hard to show. module app/other pub def unrelated : Int32 0 end
files.iyi doc Array: # The one sequence — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3. # # `Array` is a compiler-known generic class, like `String`: an array literal is # lowered to `Array(T).unsafe_build` and `to_unsafe` before any of this is # read (`LiteralExpander#expand`), so those two names are not ours to choose. # # A buffer, a size and a capacity. Growth doubles, which is the only policy # that keeps a run of `<<` linear, and there is no shrinking; `shift` steps # the buffer forward, so the capacity is what is left past it. class Array(T) # The two in order, as a new array; neither operand changes. def +(other : Array(T)) : Array(T) def <<(value : T) : Array(T) def ==(other : Array(T)) : Bool # A negative index counts from the end, so `a[-1]` is the last element. # Still out of range after that wrap (or empty) raises, same message. def [](index : Int32) : T def []=(index : Int32, value : T) : T def []?(index : Int32) : T | ::Nil def all?(& : (T -> Bool)) : Bool def any?(& : (T -> Bool)) : Bool # The elements that are not nil, in an array whose type says so: what a # list of `to_i?` answers becomes once the failures are dropped. def compact # `a.concat(a)` is a doubling, not a loop: `each` walked *other*'s growing # size while `<<` grew it, so `[1, 2].concat(itself)` grew the buffer until # the capacity arithmetic overflowed. The length is read once. def concat(other : Array(T)) : Array(T) # The questions a list gets asked with one answer. `find` answers nil # when none does, the way Crystal's does and `index` below already did. def count(& : (T -> Bool)) : Int32 # Every element equal to `value` out, answering the last or nil, as the # other library's: it took the first alone, `[1, 2, 1]` left `[2, 1]`. def delete(value : T) : T | ::Nil def dup : Array(T) def each(& : (T -> Nil)) : Nil def each_with_index(& : (T, Int32 -> Nil)) : Nil def empty? : Bool def find(& : (T -> Bool)) : T | ::Nil # The first `n`, or all of them when there are fewer: a prefix, not a # question, so it never panics. def first(n : Int32) : Array(T) # `first` on an empty array is a mistake rather than a nil: the array knows # it is empty and so does whoever wrote the call. `last?` above answers the # other question, and is the one the trait defaults use. def first : T # Hashing follows `==`, mixed as a tuple's members are (object.iyi): an # array writes `==`, so `Reference#hash` answered its type's id and every # array key shared one slot - 40,000 of them took 1.2 s to insert. def hash : Int32 def includes?(value : T) : Bool # Where a value first is, or nil. def index(value : T) : Int32 | ::Nil def inspect : String def join(separator : String) : String # Here rather than on `Enumerable`: the trait is iyi's, written in # `src/std`, and every one of its methods that returns a sequence # returns one of these. So an `Array` is what a sample ends up holding, and # `join` is what it ends up calling. # With nothing between: `["a", "b"].join` is `"ab"`. def join : String # `last` on an empty array is a mistake rather than a nil, as `first` is. def last : T def last? : T | ::Nil def map(& : (T -> U)) : Array(U) forall U # The element whose key is largest, or smallest, the first of equals; a # NaN key is above every other, as `<=>` places it. Empty is a mistake. def max_by(& : (T -> U)) : T forall U def min_by(& : (T -> U)) : T forall U def new(capacity : Int32) def new # Removes and returns the last element. Empty is a mistake, as with `last`. def pop : T def reduce(initial : U, & : (U, T -> U)) : U forall U def reject(& : (T -> Bool)) : Array(T) # A copy in the other order. def reversed : Array(T) def select(& : (T -> Bool)) : Array(T) # Removes and returns the first element. The buffer steps past it rather # than the rest moving down: moving them made draining a queue quadratic, # and `while item = queue.shift?` - how the prelude says a queue is # drained - took 1.6 s over 100,000 items. The slot stepped past is still # the buffer's chunk, which the collector keeps by the pointer into it, # and the next growth copies only what is left. def shift : T # The first element or nil, which is how a queue is drained: `while # item = queue.shift?`. def shift? : T | ::Nil def size : Int32 def sort_in_place(& : (T, T -> Int32)) : self # The pair for elements that already compare, by `<`. SPEC.md III.1.7a # pairs `sort_in_place` with `sorted` and the hint for `sort!` names both, # but only `sorted` had this form: "expected to be invoked with a block". def sort_in_place : self # Sorted on a key each element answers, ascending by `<`: the same pair # as above, one name longer. Each element's key is computed once, and the # pairs of key and element are what the merge sort orders. def sort_in_place_by(& : (T -> U)) : self forall U # The copy, with the comparison written out. One body, because the difference # between the pair is which array it runs on. The block is handed on through # `yield`, not captured: a captured block is kept to call later, and `!` in # it was refused as "maybe by a task" although the sort runs it here. def sorted(& : (T, T -> Int32)) : Array(T) def sorted : Array(T) def sorted_by(& : (T -> U)) : Array(T) forall U # The sum of the elements, and `T.zero` (src/iyi/number.iyi) when there # are none, as `std/enumerable`'s `sum` answers: this one raised "sum of # an empty array" where `Set(Int32).new.sum` was 0. `["a", "b"].sum` is a # compile error, as in the other library; `join` puts strings together. def sum : T # The sum of what the block answers for each element, and the block's # own zero when there are none. def sum(& : (T -> U)) : U forall U # `[1, 2, 3]`, the way it is written: an array printed is its elements # inspected, so a string inside keeps its quotes and a nil says so. Cast, # or `Tuple.new.to_a`'s `Array(NoReturn)` "can't infer block return type". def to_s : String # The same values as a `Set`, in the order first met. def to_set : Set(T) def to_unsafe : Pointer(T) # Each value once, in the order first met, found through a table: a # search of what was kept so far made it quadratic, 284 ms for 200,000 # elements with 10,000 distinct. def uniq : Array(T) # :nodoc: def unsafe_set_size(size : Int32) : Nil # Pairs, element by element, as many as this array holds: a shorter # *other* is refused at its first missing index, as the other library does. def zip(other : Array(U)) : Array(Tuple(T, U)) forall U # The same pairs handed to a block, with no array of them made: the # other library's `a.zip(b) { |x, y| ... }`, which a training loop calls # a few million times, and which refuses a shorter *other* the same way. def zip(other : Array(U), & : (T, U -> _)) : Nil forall U # `Array.new(729, 0)`: *size* copies of *value*, the other library's fill # form. A second argument used to be an arity error beside a one-argument # form that means capacity, which a port reads as the fill it was. def self.new(size : Int32, value : T) : Array(T) # `Array(T).new(n) { |i| ... }`: n elements, each the block's answer for # its index - a row of a grid, a table of squares. def self.new(size : Int32, & : (Int32 -> T)) : Array(T) # An array of *capacity* elements that are not written yet. The literal # expander fills them through `to_unsafe` immediately afterwards, which is # why this is allowed to hand out a size it has not stored anything at. def self.unsafe_build(capacity : Int32) : Array(T) end
files.iyi doc Atomic: # iyi: `Atomic(T)` — a word two threads may both write. SPEC.md III.4.10. # # The first thing in this prelude that assumes a second thread, and it # arrived the way everything here arrives, with a caller: the thread # floor (`bench/thread_floor.iyi`) counted its threads in and out on # three `fun`s of inline asm, and the release build's `xchg` clobbered a # register the asm had declared an input, which cost a day. These six # verbs are the compiler's own instructions instead — `atomicrmw`, # `cmpxchg`, an ordered load and an ordered store — so the register # allocation is LLVM's problem, the aarch64 arm is whatever the target's # CPU offers (`ldaxr`/`stlxr` loops, or LSE's `ldaddal` where the # machine has it), and nothing is spelled twice per architecture. The # floor holds: `nm -u` on a program that uses one names nothing new, # because a 64-bit-or-narrower atomic is an instruction on every target # iyi links for, never a `__atomic_*` call. `bench/thread_floor.sh` # asserts that, plain and release, on both Linux arms and on darwin. # # **One ordering, sequentially consistent, and no parameter to weaken # it.** This is Go's rule (its memory model makes every `sync/atomic` # operation sequentially consistent and the package has no ordering # argument) rather than C++'s or Rust's, and it is a decision, not an # omission. An ordering parameter is the part of an atomic API people # get wrong, the compiler cannot check, and a program cannot test for; # the cost of not having it is a fence on the architectures that # distinguish the orderings, and on x86_64 — the machine the floor was # measured on — a sequentially consistent `add` and a relaxed one are # the same `lock xadd`. On aarch64 the difference is `ldaddal` against # `ldadd`, and it is not yet a number: the day a profile of the marker # or the scheduler names one, that measurement is what adds the # weaker spelling, and it will be added as its own verb rather than a # parameter, so a call site says what it means. # # `T` is one of the four integers `primitives.iyi` gives arithmetic to. # A pointer or a reference is refused by name rather than admitted # untested: the arena list that will want one is the caller that will # bring it. The verbs and their answers are Crystal's, so a program that # reads the same under `--crystal` means the same: `add`, `sub` and # `swap` answer the value the word held before; `compare_and_set` # answers that value and whether the exchange happened, which is what a # retry loop needs without a second load. # # An `Atomic(T)` is a struct holding the word, so it lives where it is # declared — a class's field, a class variable, a mapping — and the # instructions address that word in place. Copying one copies a number, # not a synchronisation, which is the same contract Crystal's has. struct Atomic(T) # `word += value`; answers what the word held before. def add(value : T) : T # If the word holds `expected`, it now holds `desired`. Answers what the # word held, and whether the exchange happened; a retry loop feeds the # first back in as its next `expected`. def compare_and_set(expected : T, desired : T) : Tuple(T, Bool) # The word, read once, ordered. def get : T def new(value : T) # The word, written once, ordered. def set(value : T) : Nil # `word -= value`; answers what the word held before. def sub(value : T) : T # `word = value`; answers what the word held before. def swap(value : T) : T end

files.iyi doc Cancelled: # What a wait answers when its task was cancelled (III.4.2): an error # member. Here, not in the runtime: `IyiSocket` answers it on every target. struct Cancelled def message : String def new end
files.iyi doc Channel: # ── Channel — III.4.6 ────────────────────────────────────────────────── # # `Channel(T).new` is a rendezvous, as Crystal's is: a send completes when # a receive takes it, and either side parks until the other arrives. A # parked sender carries its value in its node's box, and a parked # receiver has a slot a sender fills, so the handoff needs no third # party; `new(capacity)` buffers that many sends first. Closing drains # what was delivered, then refuses: a parked sender whose box is still # full failed, and its value dies with the node. # # `T : Share` is not enforced yet for the reason the file header gives: # one thread cannot race, and a marker that gates nothing cannot be # tested for gating. `select` is answered by this protocol — a node per # arm, one nonce, losers stale by arithmetic until the woken select takes # them out — at the bottom of the class. class Channel(T) # Everyone parked is woken; what each wake means is read on the woken # side — a receiver finds the buffer, then `ChannelClosed`; a sender # finds its box still full. def close : Nil def closed? : Bool def new(capacity : Int32) def new # `select`'s arms park through these with one shared nonce; a plain # call parks with a fresh nonce of its own. *slot* is where a rendezvous # sender puts its value (`IyiWaiter#slot`). def park_receive_node(fiber : IyiFiber, nonce : UInt64, slot : UInt64) : IyiWaiter def park_send_node(fiber : IyiFiber, nonce : UInt64, value : T) : IyiSendNode(T) # Assumes `send_ready?`. A rendezvous puts the value in the parked # receiver's own slot (`hand`). It went into the buffer, and the send # answered delivered on the word of the wake: a select woken that way # took another arm ready by then, a receiver cancelled before it ran # answered `Cancelled`, and either way the value stayed in a channel of # no capacity after its sender left. A buffered send completes when the # buffer takes it, so there the woken receiver finds it in the buffer. def put_now(value : T) : Nil | ChannelClosed # A closed channel drains what was delivered before it refuses. A # rendezvous sender that finds this receive parked writes its value into # `got` and marks the node handed, and that is the answer even when the # task was cancelled before it ran: the sender was told it was taken. # A woken park that was handed nothing takes its node out of the queue, # so a cancelled one leaves nothing behind. def receive : T | ChannelClosed | Cancelled def receive_ready? : Bool # Nothing happens on the arm `take_now` answers: `ChannelClosed` is # the refusal here, where a closed channel's buffer is spent. def receive_refused? : Bool def receive_select_action : IyiReceiveSelect(T) def send(value : T) : Nil | ChannelClosed | Cancelled def send_ready? : Bool def send_select_action(value : T) : IyiSendSelect(T) # Assumes `receive_ready?`: the buffer, then a parked sender's box, # then the refusal. def take_now : T | ChannelClosed # Out of the receive queue from wherever it stands, in constant time, # and no longer linked anywhere; a node no queue holds is left as it # is. The queue is linked both ways because a select's losing arms # leave from the middle: they stayed until something walked them off # the head, so a loop selecting over a busy channel and an idle one # left a node in the idle one's queue for every park - 30 MiB kept # after two million rounds, freed only when the idle channel was used. def unlink_receiver(node : IyiWaiter) : Nil # The send queue's `unlink_receiver`. def unlink_sender(node : IyiSendNode(T)) : Nil # No arm ready answers -1, which the expansion's case meets with the # program's own `else`. def self.non_blocking_select(actions : U, bound : Int32) forall U # ── select — III.4.6, the library half of the expansion ──────────── # # A `select` compiles to `%i, %v, %h = ::Channel.select({arm, arm}, b)` # and a case over the index; `non_blocking_select` when an `else` arm # exists. One def serves every arity, because a tuple's size is a # compile-time fact a macro walks. `%h` says the arm's operation # happened, and an arm nobody binds runs its body only then: it ran # unless its answer was an `Error`, so a `Channel(Boom)`'s receive took # the `Boom` and skipped the body. *bound* is the first arm that binds, # -1 for none, and a cancelled task's `Cancelled` goes to it, as that # arm's own primitive would have answered it. def self.select(actions : U, bound : Int32) forall U end

files.iyi doc Char: # One character - a byte, in this prelude, which reads its strings as ASCII. struct Char < Value def !=(other : Char) : Bool # The character *other* code points on: what `'a'..'z'` steps by. `chr` # refuses a surrogate too, where `'\u{D7FF}' + 1` was U+D800. def +(other : Int32) : Char def <(other : Char) : Bool def <=(other : Char) : Bool def ==(other : Char) : Bool def >(other : Char) : Bool def >=(other : Char) : Bool def alphanumeric? : Bool def bytesize : Int32 def digit? : Bool # `0x10FFFF` is the last code point there is; past it a `'?'` goes out # rather than a sequence no reader can decode. `String::Builder` writes # these too, which had its own copy of the four arms. def each_byte(& : (UInt8 -> Nil)) : Nil def hash : Int32 def inspect : String # Itself as `inspect` writes it between *quote*s, the other library's # escapes; not `printable?`, as `\u` and hex. `'\''` was `'''`. def inspect_into(io : String::Builder, quote : Char) : String::Builder # The classes a word counter asks about, ASCII's: a letter is one of the # fifty-two, a digit one of the ten. Whitespace is the other library's: # the space and `\t` to `\r`, and above ASCII Unicode's Zs, Zl and Zp, so # U+00A0 and U+3000 are and U+0085, a control, is not. It was ASCII's. def letter? : Bool def ord : Int32 # Not a control (Cc), format (Cf) or private-use (Co) character of # Unicode 15, nor whitespace but the space: the other library's. def printable? : Bool def to_s : String def whitespace? : Bool end

files.iyi doc Enum: # What an `enum` can do — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3. # # The compiler gives an enum exactly two methods: `value`, the integer the # member was numbered with, and `new`, which wraps one (`EnumType#initialize`). # Everything a program does with an enum is the library's, and until # `samples/iyi/enums.iyi` asked there was none of it — so the answers were # `Object`'s: `Level::Warn == Level::Warn` was **false**, `to_s` printed the # type's name, and `case level when Level::Warn` matched nothing, because a # `when` naming a member lowers to `Level::Warn === level` and `===` is `==`. # The compiler's own per-member question methods (`level.warn?`) call that # same `==`, and a `@[Flags]` enum's call `includes?`, so those were broken by # one gap apiece. # # `Enum` is predefined — it is what every enum's ancestor is, created before a # prelude line is read — so this reopens it the way `Range` and `String` are # reopened rather than declaring it. # # Read off the type at each instantiation: a method here is stencilled onto the # enum that calls it, so `@type` is that enum and `@type.constants` are its # members. Nothing walks a table at run time and nothing is allocated to answer # a name: `to_s` is a `case` over integers the compiler folds. struct Enum < Value def &(other : self) : self # An order, because a level is a threshold: `level >= Level::Info` is the # first thing a program writes after a `case`. Four operators rather than a # `Comparable` include — the prelude has no such module, and a trait would be # `std/traits`' to carry (SPEC.md II.6). def <(other : self) : Bool def <=(other : self) : Bool # Equality is the value's, which is what makes every other name work: `!=` # and `===` are `Object`'s and both read this, `case` lowers to `===`, and # the question methods the compiler writes are `self == Member`. def ==(other : self) : Bool def >(other : self) : Bool def >=(other : self) : Bool # A key in a `Hash` is hashed and then compared, so a type used as one owes # both (`src/iyi/hash.iyi`). The value's own hash: `to_i32` panicked past it. def hash : Int32 # Whether every bit of *other* is in this one, which is what a `@[Flags]` # enum's question methods ask: the compiler writes `mode.read?` as # `self.includes?(Mode::Read)`. def includes?(other : self) : Bool # `#{Level::Warn.inspect}` is the member written down rather than printed, # and for an enum the two are the same text. It is here because `Object`'s # sends it back to `to_s` — which was the type's name — and a sample that # inspects a `Level?` was reading that. def inspect : String # The member's name, and the value's digits where no member has it — # `Level.new(9).to_s` is `"9"`, which is what a value off a wire prints as. # # A flags enum answers with a member's name when one has its value (`None` # for zero, `All` for every bit, which was skipped), else the names of the # bits it holds, each named once, and the rest as a number: `Read | 8`. def to_s : String # The two set operators a flags enum is built to be used with. `Mode::Read | # Mode::Write` is how one is written down, and `mode & Mode::Write` is how a # bit is taken out of it. def |(other : self) : self # A member from the integer it was numbered with, or `nil` where no member # has it. `new` takes any value of the base type by design — that is how an # enum comes back from C or off a wire — and this is the question that asks # whether the one in hand is a member. def self.from_value?(value : Int) : self | ::Nil # The same list said in text, which is what a message naming the choices # needs: `"one of #{Level.names.join(", ")}"`. def self.names : Array(String) # A member read back from text, or `nil` where no member has that name. What # a program does with an argument or a configuration line, so the comparison # is the lenient one a person types: `"warn"`, `"Warn"` and `"WARN"` all # answer `Level::Warn`, and nothing else does. # # `nil` rather than a panic, because the text is somebody else's input and # the caller is the only thing that knows what to say about it (III.1). def self.parse?(name : String) : self | ::Nil # Every member, in the order they were written. A menu, a validation table, # a loop that has to reach all of them — and for a flags enum the members # rather than `None` and `All`, which are the compiler's own. def self.values : Array(self) end

files.iyi doc Float64: struct Float64 < Float def !=(other : Int32) : Bool def !=(other : Int64) : Bool def !=(other : UInt8) : Bool def !=(other : UInt64) : Bool def !=(other : Float64) : Bool def *(other : Int32) : self def *(other : Int64) : self def *(other : UInt8) : self def *(other : UInt64) : self def *(other : Float64) : self # A whole power by squaring in double-double - the power and the base each # a sum of two doubles good to some 106 bits - rounded once, at the end. # In plain doubles every step rounded: `1.1 ** 100` was 13780.612339822364 # and `0.9999999 ** 10000000` 854,604 ulp off. A negative exponent powers # the reciprocal, itself a pair, so `2.0 ** -1074` is 5.0e-324 although # `2.0 ** 1074` is infinite, and `Int32::MIN` is counted in an Int64. def **(exponent : Int32) : Float64 def +(other : Int32) : self def +(other : Int64) : self def +(other : UInt8) : self def +(other : UInt64) : self def +(other : Float64) : self def -(other : Int32) : self def -(other : Int64) : self def -(other : UInt8) : self def -(other : UInt64) : self def -(other : Float64) : self def /(other : Float64) : Float64 def <(other : Int32) : Bool def <(other : Int64) : Bool def <(other : UInt8) : Bool def <(other : UInt64) : Bool def <(other : Float64) : Bool def <=(other : Int32) : Bool def <=(other : Int64) : Bool def <=(other : UInt8) : Bool def <=(other : UInt64) : Bool def <=(other : Float64) : Bool def ==(other : Int32) : Bool def ==(other : Int64) : Bool def ==(other : UInt8) : Bool def ==(other : UInt64) : Bool def ==(other : Float64) : Bool def >(other : Int32) : Bool def >(other : Int64) : Bool def >(other : UInt8) : Bool def >(other : UInt64) : Bool def >(other : Float64) : Bool def >=(other : Int32) : Bool def >=(other : Int64) : Bool def >=(other : UInt8) : Bool def >=(other : UInt64) : Bool def >=(other : Float64) : Bool # The sign cleared, which a comparison cannot do: `-0.0 < 0.0` is false, # and `(-0.0).abs` answered `-0.0` - `log10(-0.0)` came out `+Infinity` # for it. `copysign` is an instruction on every target. def abs : Float64 def ceil : Float64 def fdiv(other : Int32) : self def fdiv(other : Int64) : self def fdiv(other : UInt8) : self def fdiv(other : UInt64) : self def fdiv(other : Float64) : self # The integer below and above, as a `Float64`: one instruction where the # processor has it (`IyiRounding`), the conversion below where it does # not. Past 2^52 every double is an integer already and is answered as # it is, as NaN and the infinities are; the conversion is exact under # it. The answer carries the argument's sign, which is where a zero's # comes from - `(-0.3).ceil` is `-0.0`, as the instruction and the other # library answer. def floor : Float64 # `-0.0 == 0.0`, so they hash alike. It was `std/float`'s, and a # `Hash(Float64, V)` without that import put every key in one slot. def hash : Int32 # To `digits` places, a tie to the even one: scaled, rounded, scaled # back, so `3.14159.round(2)` is the double nearest 3.14. A negative # `digits` rounds to tens, hundreds, ...: `1234.0.round(-2)` is 1200.0, # and `25.0.round(-1)` is 20.0. The scale for those divides first rather # than multiplying by a fraction, which no double spells exactly. # # Where the scale leaves a double's range the answer is at hand, and the # arithmetic made Infinity or NaN of it: a double at 2^52 or past has no # fraction to round (`1e308.round(1)` was Infinity), a scale past the # range keeps every digit a double has (`1.5.round(400)` was NaN), and # one past the range the other way is a zero (`1.5.round(-400)`). # # A scaled value at 2^53 or past is at hand the same way: the place # `digits` names is finer than the double's last bit, so the nearest # double to the rounded decimal is the double itself. Scaled back, it # moved: `0.8173247445520655.round(17)` was 0.8173247445520654, and # `(-0.05).round(300)`, whose scale `10.0 ** 300` is not 10^300 exactly, # was -0.049999999999999996. Between 2^52 and 2^53 the place can still # be the coarser one, so that band is scaled back as before. def round(digits : Int32) : Float64 # The nearest integer, a tie to the even one — Crystal's `round`, so the # name means one thing in both libraries (SPEC.md III.1.7a): `2.5.round` # is 2.0 and `3.5.round` is 4.0. `std/number` names the other modes. # The magnitude's fraction decides, not a sum: `(x + 0.5).floor` rounded # the sum first, and 0.49999999999999994 + 0.5 is 1.0. The sign goes # back by a multiplication, so `(-0.25).round` is -0.0, as there. A zero # is its own nearest integer and is answered as it is: `-0.0 < 0.0` is # false, and the sign test below answered `(-0.0).round` as 0.0. def round : Float64 def to_f : Float64 def to_f64 : Float64 # The checked form raises on overflow — which in this prelude is a panic, # since `__crystal_raise_overflow` prints and exits (SPEC.md III.1.4). # # The unchecked form is the conversion without the check, and a float # past the range saturates (NaN is 0), alike in every build. It is # spelled the way `unsafe_chr` below is: `unsafe_to_u8`. Crystal spells # it `to_u8!`, which is not a name in iyi (SPEC.md III.1.7) — those # declarations were accepted only because a macro expansion was # reparsed by the other language's rules, and no iyi source could call # one: `x.to_u8!` is `x.to_u8` with its error propagated. The callers # wanted the instruction: `memset`'s `value.to_u8!` is C's "converted to # unsigned char", and the checked form panics on 0x1ff where C writes 0xff. def to_i : Int32 def to_i32 : Int32 def to_i64 : Int64 def to_s : String def to_u64 : UInt64 def to_u8 : UInt8 def unsafe_to_f : Float64 def unsafe_to_f64 : Float64 def unsafe_to_i : Int32 def unsafe_to_i32 : Int32 def unsafe_to_i64 : Int64 def unsafe_to_u64 : UInt64 def unsafe_to_u8 : UInt8 def self.zero : self end
files.iyi doc Hash: # The one dictionary — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3. # # Two dense arrays in insertion order, keys and values, and an index over # them: open addressing with linear probing from the key's hash to the # position of its entry, `-1` where a slot is free. The compact layout # Python's dictionary and the other library's `Hash` both settled on: # iteration follows the order things went in - the order a word count # prints its words - and the index is one array of integers rather than a # copy of the keys. Deletion marks the entry gone and its index slot a # tombstone, `-2`, which a probe steps over and an insert may take; the # dense arrays close their gaps when they next grow. Closing the gap at # once and rebuilding the index emptied a set of 20,000 in 0.95 s. # # Hashing is `key.hash`, defined per type in this prelude, and not iyi's # `Hashable` trait: that lives in `src/std`, the opt-in library, and a # prelude that depended on it would have the dependency backwards. class Hash(K, V) def [](key : K) : V def []=(key : K, value : V) : V def []?(key : K) : V | ::Nil # The value the key had, or nil. The entry is marked gone where it # stands, so the order of what remains is the order it went in, and its # index slot becomes a tombstone. `each` starts past the gone at the # front: from entry 0, taking the oldest key and deleting it until none # was left stepped over every one gone before, 197 ms for 40,000. def delete(key : K) : V | ::Nil # Every pair, in the order it went in. def each(& : (K, V -> Nil)) : Nil def empty? : Bool def has_key?(key : K) : Bool def inspect : String # The keys, and the values, each in the order they went in. def keys : Array(K) def new def new(&block : (Hash(K, V), K -> V)) def size : Int32 # Every pair as a tuple, in the order it went in - what a sort by value # starts from. def to_a : Array(Tuple(K, V)) # `{"a" => 1}`, in insertion order, both sides inspected; a first key in # braces is spaced off, `{ {1, 2} => 3 }`, as a tuple's: `{{` is a macro. def to_s : String def values : Array(V) def self.new(default : V) : Hash(K, V) end

A negative exponent is a # mistake for an integer, as division by zero is. def **(exponent : Int32) : Int32 def +(other : Int32) : self def +(other : Int64) : self def +(other : UInt8) : self def +(other : UInt64) : self def +(other : Float64) : Float64 def -(other : Int32) : self def -(other : Int64) : self def -(other : UInt8) : self def -(other : UInt64) : self def -(other : Float64) : Float64 def - : Int32 def /(other : Float64) : Float64 # The zero is checked here rather than left to the processor. `1 // 0` used # to reach `unsafe_div`, trap, and kill the program with "Process terminated # because of a floating-point system exception" — an integer division # reported by the operating system as a floating-point fault, which is a # sentence nobody can act on. def //(other : Int32) : Int32 def <(other : Int32) : Bool def <(other : Int64) : Bool def <(other : UInt8) : Bool def <(other : UInt64) : Bool def <(other : Float64) : Bool def <(other : UInt16) : Bool # Shifts, and the magnitude: what a bit of arithmetic past the four # operators asks for first.
